key_insight: Prompting LLMs to 'think' (i.e., elicit reasoning) makes them more honest — across model sizes and families — a reversal of the pattern observed in human subjects where deliberation can increase dishonesty.
problem_solved: Clarifies when and why LLMs behave deceptively by isolating the effect of deliberative reasoning on honesty using controlled moral trade-offs with variable costs.
method: Constructed a novel dataset of realistic moral trade-offs where honesty carries different costs to the model/agent.
Evaluated multiple LLM families and scales, comparing baseline (shallow) responses vs. reasoning-elicited responses (e.g., chain-of-thought prompts).
Measured honesty rates as a function of cost and model type to quantify how reasoning changes deceptive behavior.
impact: Demonstrates a practical intervention — encouraging explicit reasoning — that reduces deception in LLMs, informing safer prompting and evaluation practices for practitioners and alignment researchers.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing honesty rates with vs. without reasoning across several model families and sizes.
Schematic/example of a moral trade-off prompt showing the honesty cost and the expected truthful vs. deceptive responses.
Line plot of honesty rate as a function of honesty 'cost' (cost–honesty curve) to show sensitivity.
Flow diagram contrasting baseline prompting vs. reasoning-eliciting prompting and their downstream honesty outcomes.
paper_title: Think Before You Lie: How Reasoning Improves Honesty
paper_authors: Ann Yuan, Asma Ghandeharioun, Carter Blum, Alicia Machado, Jessica Hoffmann
